titleStmt.title: Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State

div.head: 405. Telegram From the Embassy in Paraguay to the Department of State
div.p: 2. Summary: During a lengthy and relaxed conversation, President Stroessner confided to me about his health, his attitude toward reelection in 1988, concerns about Bolivia, and the change in U.S. Ambassadors here. He displayed a vigor which belies public questions about the state of his health. End summary.

3. After having been informed by ForMin Saldivar on Monday that President Stroessner would be too busy to receive me this week, I was advised on Wednesday (August 21) that he wanted to see me the next morning. Thus, I had the opportunity for a lengthy tour d’horizon, which the President said he wanted.

4. Health: Stroessner raised this issue by pointing to a scratch on his hand and saying he wanted me to know it was from an accident, and that he was having no further skin problems. I noted that the city was abuzz with rumors about a possible gallbladder operation. He confirmed that his doctors told him he needed an operation, that although it was not urgent, it should be done soon and that he would have it here in Asuncion. He later returned to his health saying that he sometimes lacks pep (falta animo) in the morning when he wakes up, but that the thought that people are waiting to see him in his office gets him moving.

5. Reelection: Stroessner commented, in the context of speculation about his candidacy for reelection in 1988, that he lives in the present, not the future. He is interested in serving, he said, as long as “God, my health and the Paraguayan people allow me to.” (Comment: He later reiterated he would serve “as long as the Paraguayan people want me.” This is a switch from his past line that he would serve as
long as the Colorado Party wanted him as its candidate. This may be an intended or unconscious reflection of the fact that he is currently facing some independent jockeying for position within the party. End comment.)

6. Contacts with Colorados: I knew from Interior Minister Montanaro that the President was interested in learning details of my contacts with various elements of the Colorado Party. Stroessner raised the issue anew and wanted to know why I would waste time meeting with what he described as an unimportant group of Colorado Party legislators, which, he pointed out, included people who were “not disciplined.” He knew I was going to have some of the “kamikaze” group (the Frutos clan) to lunch on Friday.

7. I said that it was important that I be able to inform Washington accurately on all political currents here. In that context I mentioned that I planned to lunch the following week with Mario Abdo Benitez (who is at the forefront of the opposite “militant” faction). The President asked, in the same tone as previously, “Why are you meeting with him?” I went through the same explanation again, probably to no avail. (Comment: This is a sensitive area for him. It is extremely clear that he spends a great deal of time U.S. Embassy watching. End comment.)

8. Change of Ambassadors: Stroessner said in terms of the upcoming change of Ambassadors that Ambassador-designate Taylor “could be valuable here.” He mentioned his narcotics program direction experience. I assured him that Taylor is a well-rounded career officer, not just a narcotics specialist.

9. Military assistance: Stroessner said that Paraguay could use the resumption of foreign military sales from the U.S. he spoke of the military imbalance between Bolivia and Paraguay and referred to the historical context of the Chaco War. The U.S. sale of a patrol craft to the Bolivians also came up, with Stroessner pointing out that the ship is now visiting in the Asuncion port. The threat is growing, he said. I used that opportunity to once again explain to the President that as long as his government continues to take actions such as closing the ABC Color newspaper and taking Radio Nanduti off the air that there will be no disposition in Washington to resuming this kind of military assistance.

10. Exchange rate: As I was leaving, I remarked on the skyrocketing value of the dollar compared to the
guarani. He replied abruptly that there would be no devaluation of the currency. I understand from other well-connected sources that the President has said he will not replace MinFin Barrientos. This conversation coincided with the unprecedented leap in the dollar-guarani exchange rate from about 1:800 on August 19 to 1:1050 and approaching 1100 on August 21. The President appeared not to understand that the outside world could and was devaluing the guarani.

11. Comment: Stroessner was the most relaxed and voluble I have seen him. He did not seem overly preoccupied by his health, beyond a normal focus on the aging process. A bit of bile entered the conversation in terms of my meeting with Colorado Party dissidents and the GOP’s handling of media criticism. In general, however, Stroessner’s vital signs show little indication that he is losing his grip although his economic blindspot remains as glaring as ever.

note.p: Source: Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D850599–0102. Secret; Immediate; Exdis.

In telegram 4295 from Asuncion, August 19, the Embassy reported on rumors of gall bladder surgery for Stroessner. (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D850588–0608)

In telegram 2799 from Asuncion, July 12, 1983 the Embassy wrote: “The Paraguayan Government July 9 closed down a local radio station, Radio Nanduti, for 30 days, accusing the station of having ‘disturbed the public order.’”(Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D830395–0406) In telegram 7179 from Asuncion, November 8, the Embassy reported: “The Paraguayan authorities moved once again against Humberto Rubin, owner of the popular radio station Radio Nanduti. On November 6 the telecommunications authorities prohibited Rubin from working as an announcer. The move came on the heels of a meeting between Rubin and the Under Secretary for Information, Anibal Fernandez, who, according to Rubin, warned him that if he did not stop interviewing leaders of the unrecognized opposition parties and otherwise providing so much coverage to their activities, his station would have to close.” (Department of State, Central Foreign Policy File, Electronic Telegrams, D840716–0281)
